o: Cervical and lumbar costal elements have no separate bony centre
They ossify by extension from the neural arch; an occasional centre at C7 or L1 gives a cervical or lumbar rib. (Last's p. 558)
The sacral costal elements have no bony centres
The weight-bearing sacral costal elements have centres, appearing at 6 months of fetal life. (Last's p. 558)
The atlas ossifies from a centre in each lateral mass in the seventh week
They unite posteriorly at 4 years; an anterior arch centre appears at 1 year. (Last's p. 558)
The secondary centre for the tip of the dens fuses at about 3 years
It appears at about 3 and fuses at 12; the dens joins the body at 3. (Last's p. 558)
The anterior arch–lateral mass junction may permanently divide the upper atlas facet
It crosses the front of the upper articular surface and fuses at 7 years. (Last's p. 558)
The epiphyseal ring for the lower axis body fuses in the early teens
It appears at puberty and fuses at about 25. (Last's p. 558)
Mamillary processes of T12 and the lumbar vertebrae have secondary centres
They appear after puberty and fuse in the early twenties. (Last's p. 558)
The sacral costal centres fuse with the neural arches at about 12 years
They fuse with the arches at about 5 years and with the bodies in the early twenties. (Last's p. 558)
The primary curvature is retained in the thoracic, sacral and coccygeal regions
Secondary lordoses develop in the cervical and lumbar regions after birth. (Last's p. 535-6)
Last's says the curves are the main shock absorbers of the column
The bends give resilience, but the shock-absorbing factors are the discs. (Last's p. 536)
Thoracic costal facets on the body lie on the neural arch

The neurocentral junction lies in front of them.
So the centrum is not the anatomical body. (Last's p. 536)
The foramen transversarium is formed by the true transverse process
It is produced by the costal element. (Last's p. 536)
Last's says "costotransverse bar" is a wrong name for the costal lamella
It is the intertubercular lamella between anterior and posterior tubercles. (Last's p. 536-7)
A smooth bony cervical rib causes more symptoms than a fibrous band

A thin fibrous band may be more irritating.
Symptoms usually appear around puberty. (Last's p. 537)
A well-developed cervical rib is associated with a prefixed brachial plexus
That preserves the normal nerve-to-rib relationship. (Last's p. 537)
The lumbar "transverse processes" are true transverse processes
They are costal elements; the true process is reduced to the mamillary process and accessory tubercle. (Last's p. 537)
The sacral auricular surface lies wholly on the lateral mass
So morphologically the pelvis articulates with ribs. (Last's p. 537)
Annulus fibres lie at 60–75° to the vertebral bodies
They lie at 25–45°, with alternate layers at right angles. (Last's p. 537)
In the adult the nucleus pulposus lies nearest the back of the disc
Because growth occurs ventrally and laterally. (Last's p. 538)
The notochord originally extended only to the foramen magnum
It extended as far as the sella turcica. (Last's p. 537)

questions.s: Concerning the joints between vertebral bodies (Last's):
o: Last's says the uncovertebral "joints" are not synovial

Small cavities form there from degenerative changes in the disc.
They occur on C3–7 and T1. (Last's p. 539)
The anterior longitudinal ligament narrows as it descends
It broadens gradually downwards; the posterior ligament narrows downwards. (Last's p. 539)
The posterior longitudinal ligament is loosely attached over the bodies to let basivertebral veins exit
It is broadest and firmly attached over the discs. (Last's p. 539)
The anterior longitudinal ligament begins at the body of the axis
It begins at the anterior tubercle of the atlas; the posterior ligament begins at the back of the axis body. (Last's p. 539)

questions.s: Concerning the joints between neural arches (Last's):
o: Each facet joint is supplied by the nerve of its own level and the one above
So one nerve supplies two joints. (Last's p. 539)
The ligamenta flava attach to the back of the upper lamina and front of the lower
They attach to the front of the upper lamina and the back of the lower. (Last's p. 539)
The erector spinae are electrically silent when the spine is fully flexed
The taut supraspinous ligaments then support the spine. (Last's p. 539)
The interspinous ligaments are best developed in the cervical region
They are well developed only in the lumbar region. (Last's p. 539)
The spinal curvatures are produced mostly by the wedge shape of the discs
Partly by the wedge-shaped bodies. (Last's p. 540)
In spondylolisthesis the lamina of L5 is deficient
Last's: the pedicle of L5 is deficient, so bony locking at the facet joint fails. (Last's p. 540)
In the cervical region part of the body below the disc bounds the intervertebral foramen
The pedicle arises a little lower down the back of the body. (Last's p. 540)
The vertebral canal enlarges from above downwards
It becomes progressively smaller from above downwards. (Last's p. 540)
Rotation occurs mainly in the thoracic region

Last's calls this strange.
Lumbar rotation is almost absent. (Last's p. 540, 543)
The T12/L1 facet joints are thoracic in type
They are lumbar in type. (Last's p. 540)
Below about T9 thoracic rotation becomes negligible
Possibly because of the attachments of external oblique. (Last's p. 540)
Thoracic extension crowds the ribs together
Extension spreads the ribs (inspiratory); flexion crowds them (expiratory). (Last's p. 540)
The lower facet of the atlas lateral mass is round and flat
The upper facet is kidney-shaped and concave. (Last's p. 541)
Last's describes the dens as the centrum of the atlas
Long believed to be so, it "appears from comparative studies to be a development in its own right." (Last's p. 541)
The dens bears no weight
Skull weight passes through the atlas lateral masses to the superior articular processes of the axis. (Last's p. 541)
The axis spine is large because of the attachment of semispinalis capitis
It receives semispinalis cervicis below and the suboccipital muscles above. (Last's p. 541)
The lateral margin of the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane sometimes ossifies
This converts the vertebral artery groove into a foramen. (Last's p. 542)
The anterior atlanto-occipital membrane is deficient laterally for the vertebral artery
The anterior membrane closes the space completely; the posterior one is deficient laterally. (Last's p. 542)
The head weighs over 3 kg

Its centre of gravity lies in front of the joint.
Semispinalis capitis tone holds it. (Last's p. 542)
Some rotation occurs at the atlanto-occipital joints
No rotation is possible; the egg-shaped surfaces allow nodding and lateral flexion only. (Last's p. 542)
The tectorial membrane attaches to the anterior half of the foramen magnum
The spinal dura is firmly attached to it. (Last's p. 542)
The apical ligament is the strongest of the dens ligaments
It is weak; the alar ligaments are very strong and limit rotation. (Last's p. 542)
A synovial bursa separates the cruciform ligament from the dens
It is surrounded by a loose fibrous capsule. (Last's p. 542)
Rotation at the atlantoaxial joints is mainly by trapezius
The chief rotators are sternocleidomastoid, splenius capitis and inferior oblique. (Last's p. 543)
The external vertebral plexus is absent over the fronts of the bodies
It is intramuscular. (Last's p. 543)
Basivertebral veins drain into the external plexus
They drain into the internal vertebral plexus. (Last's p. 543)
In the neck the vertebral plexuses communicate with the inferior thyroid veins
Via the brachiocephalic veins; a route for thyroid metastasis. (Last's p. 543)
The neck extensors are supplied mainly by the vertebral artery
They are supplied by the occipital, deep cervical and transverse cervical arteries. (Last's p. 543)
The extensor mass is the only muscle in the body supplied by posterior rami
It derives from the outer layer of the body wall. (Last's p. 544)
The rotatores are best developed in the lumbar region
They are confined to the thoracic spine, the only region of pure rotation. (Last's p. 544)
Multifidus fibres reach spinous processes two or three vertebrae above
It extends from the upper sacrum to the upper neck. (Last's p. 544)
Semispinalis thoracis inserts two or three vertebrae higher
Each part inserts six or more vertebrae higher. (Last's p. 544)

questions.s: Concerning semispinalis capitis and erector spinae (Last's):
o: Semispinalis capitis arises from the upper six thoracic and lower four cervical transverse processes
It is the chief extensor of the head. (Last's p. 544)
Semispinalis capitis lies superficial to splenius
It lies beneath splenius and trapezius. (Last's p. 544-5)
Like soleus, semispinalis capitis contains a large venous plexus
The deep cervical artery passes in front of it. (Last's p. 545)
Iliocostalis inserts into the tips of the lower six transverse processes
It inserts by shining tendons into the angles of the lower six ribs. (Last's p. 545)
Longissimus capitis inserts into the mastoid process deep to splenius capitis
It overlies the lateral border of semispinalis capitis. (Last's p. 545)
Splenius cervicis inserts into the transverse processes of the lower cervical vertebrae
It inserts into the upper three or four, deep to levator scapulae. (Last's p. 546)
Spinalis is the most medial part of erector spinae
It is small and blends with semispinalis. (Last's p. 546)
Last's says the cervical part of iliocostalis reaches the upper cervical transverse processes
It reaches the transverse processes of the lower four cervical vertebrae. (Last's p. 545)

questions.s: Concerning the back of the neck (Last's):
o: The ligamentum nuchae is attached to the investing layer of deep fascia
Its three borders attach to the external occipital crest, the bifid spines and the investing fascia. (Last's p. 546)
The greater occipital nerve emerges through the floor of the suboccipital triangle
The suboccipital (C1) nerve emerges through the floor; the greater occipital crosses the roof. (Last's p. 546)
Rectus capitis posterior major rotates the head towards its own side

It also extends the head.
Last's says it is badly named, being oblique. (Last's p. 546)
The superior oblique arises from the spine of the axis

It arises from the back of the lateral mass of the atlas.
The inferior oblique arises from the axis spine. (Last's p. 546)

questions.s: Concerning the suboccipital muscles and vessels (Last's):
o: Rectus capitis posterior minor is the only muscle attached to the posterior arch of the atlas
It inserts into the medial area below the inferior nuchal line. (Last's p. 546)
The suboccipital muscles have large motor units
They have about five muscle fibres per motor unit and many spindles. (Last's p. 547)
Between the axis and atlas the vertebral artery has a posterior convexity
It takes up slack during rotation. (Last's p. 547)
The vertebral veins accompany the vertebral arteries into the skull
They exist only in the neck; one leaves with the artery from C6, one alone through C7. (Last's p. 547)
The spines of T5–8 lie opposite the rib tubercles two lower in the series
The upper four and lower thoracic spines lie opposite ribs one lower. (Last's p. 548)
The vertebra prominens is always C7
It may be T1, so spines should be counted up from the L4–5 space. (Last's p. 548)
The middle four thoracic bodies often show a left-sided aortic excavation
From T4 down the bodies are heart-shaped. (Last's p. 548)
The upper border of a thoracic pedicle lies below the upper surface of the body
It is level with it, so the body takes no part in the foramen above. (Last's p. 549)
The upper six transverse costal facets are concave
The lower ones are flat. (Last's p. 550)
The lower border of a thoracic lamina is grooved on its posterior surface
The upper border is grooved posteriorly, the lower border anteriorly, for the imbricated ligamenta flava. (Last's p. 549)
The superior costotransverse ligament attaches to the lower margin of the transverse process

It comes from the neck of the rib below.
A levator costae arises there too. (Last's p. 550)
The spinous processes are most steeply inclined at T12
Inclination increases to T7, then levels out to almost horizontal at T12. (Last's p. 548)
The T1 body helps form the intervertebral foramen above it
Its pedicle is attached below the upper margin as in cervical vertebrae; this foramen transmits C8. (Last's p. 550)
T12 carries its single costal facet near the upper margin of the pedicle
T11's single facet is on the upper pedicle; T12's is near the lower margin. (Last's p. 550)
The inferior articular facet of T12 is lumbar in type
Its superior facet is typically thoracic. (Last's p. 550)
Psoas minor arises below the attachment of psoas major
Psoas major begins at the lower border of T12; psoas minor arises just above this. (Last's p. 550)
The normal lumbar lordosis is produced by the discs rather than the bodies
Piled dry bodies often make a backward convexity. (Last's p. 550)
In L5 the four articular processes form a vertical rectangle
L1–2 form a vertical rectangle; L4 a square; L5 a horizontal rectangle. (Last's p. 550)
The upper facets of L4 and L5 face posteriorly as well as medially
The lumbar facets are sections of a vertical cylinder. (Last's p. 551)
Psoas is attached to the concavity of the lumbar bodies
It attaches to the upper and lower borders, spanning the concavity on a fibrous arch. (Last's p. 551)
The groove between mamillary process and accessory tubercle carries the medial branch of the posterior ramus
They represent the true transverse process. (Last's p. 551)
The lumbar vertebral canal is circular in section
It is somewhat triangular; thoracic canals are almost circular. (Last's p. 551)
The arcuate ligaments attach to the ridge on the L1 transverse process
Psoas lies medial and quadratus lumborum lateral to the ridge. (Last's p. 551)
Fusion of L5 with the sacrum is called lumbarization
It is called sacralization. (Last's p. 552)
The upper surface of S1 slopes down at 30° or more
The L5 facets on the sacrum lie as a vertical concave cylinder. (Last's p. 552)
The medial three-quarters of each anterior sacral foramen is costal in origin
Only the medial boundary is vertebral body; the other three-quarters is costal. (Last's p. 552)
Piriformis arises from the three ridges between the anterior foramina
And from the nearby lateral mass. (Last's p. 552)
Peritoneum covers the front of the lower three sacral bodies
It covers the upper two; the rectum lies against the lower three. (Last's p. 552)

questions.s: Concerning the back of the sacrum (Last's):
o: The sacral hiatus results from failure of fusion of the laminae of S5 and often S4
It is closed by the superficial (dorsal) sacrococcygeal ligament. (Last's p. 553)
The intermediate sacral crest represents the fused transverse processes
It represents fused articular processes and ends below as the sacral cornu; the lateral crest is the fused transverse processes. (Last's p. 553)
The posterior sacral foramina are enclosed wholly by the fused vertebrae
The fused costal elements lie lateral to the lateral sacral crest. (Last's p. 553)
The lateral sacral crest meets the lateral border of the sacrum at S2
It meets it at S4, the apex of the small triangular area below the auricular surface. (Last's p. 553)
Part of the sacrotuberous ligament arises from the triangular area below the auricular surface
With its attached gluteus maximus; the sacrospinous ligament and coccygeus attach below this. (Last's p. 554)
On the ala the obturator nerve lies medial to the lumbosacral trunk
The sympathetic trunk crosses the base of the ala; lateral to it lie the lumbosacral trunk medially, obturator nerve laterally, and the iliolumbar artery. (Last's p. 554)
The sacral posterior root ganglia lie inside the intervertebral foramina between the sacral pedicles
The dural root sheaths unite just distal to the ganglia. (Last's p. 554)
In the male the ala is wider than the body of S1
The body is wider than the ala in the male, narrower in the female. (Last's p. 554)
The auricular surface spans two and a half vertebrae in the male
Only two in the female. (Last's p. 554)
The S5 foramen is completed by the deep dorsal sacrococcygeal ligament
It is completed by the lateral sacrococcygeal ligament, which may ossify and give five foramina. (Last's p. 554)
The tip of the coccyx gives attachment to the intermediate part of the external anal sphincter
And to the anococcygeal raphe. (Last's p. 554)
The sacrococcygeal joint is always a synovial joint
It is a small symphysis with a disc, occasionally synovial. (Last's p. 554)
The cervical vertebral body is the same size as, or smaller than, the vertebral foramen
It is broad and kidney-shaped. (Last's p. 555)
Cervical basivertebral foramina are closer together than thoracic ones
They are wider apart than in thoracic and lumbar vertebrae. (Last's p. 555)
The posterior tubercle of a cervical transverse process is part of the costal element
Only the proximal part of the posterior bar is the true transverse element. (Last's p. 555)
Last's endorses the term costotransverse bar for the plate joining the tubercles
It is the intertubercular lamella, "frequently but wrongly" called the costotransverse bar. (Last's p. 555)
The anterior tubercles enlarge progressively from C3 to C6
C6 is the carotid tubercle (of Chassaignac). (Last's p. 555)
The posterior root ganglion lies in front of the vertebral artery
It lies behind the artery on the intertubercular lamella. (Last's p. 555)
Scalenus posterior arises from the posterior tubercles of C5 and C6
And sometimes C7; levator scapulae from those down to C4. (Last's p. 555)
Scalenus medius arises from the anterior tubercles
It arises from the posterior tubercles; longus capitis, scalenus anterior and longus colli use the anterior tubercles. (Last's p. 555)
The foramen transversarium of C7 contains the posterior vein when the vertebral vein is doubled
It does not transmit the vertebral artery. (Last's p. 556)
Last's accepts that the C7 foramen transmits the grey ramus to C7
Last's says this is doubtful. (Last's p. 556)
Scalenus pleuralis attaches to the small anterior tubercle of C7
So does the suprapleural membrane. (Last's p. 556)
The upper facets of a typical cervical vertebra face up and forward
They face obliquely up and back; the lower ones face down and forward. (Last's p. 556)
A tubercle in the "hilum" of each upper facet attaches the transverse ligament
The upper facets are kidney-shaped. (Last's p. 556)
The groove for the vertebral artery reliably orients a loose atlas
It is often shallow, and a similar groove for the C2 ganglion may lie below. (Last's p. 556)
All the bone anterior and lateral to the atlas foramen transversarium is costal
There are usually no distinct tubercles. (Last's p. 556)
Rectus capitis posterior major arises from the posterior arch of the atlas
Minor arises from dimples there; major arises from the axis spine. (Last's p. 556-7)
The internal jugular vein lies on the transverse process of the atlas
It is crossed there by the accessory nerve. (Last's p. 556)
A synovial joint lies between the back of the dens and the transverse ligament
Only a bursa lies there. (Last's p. 557)
The tectorial membrane attaches to the back of the axis body below the cruciform ligament
It sweeps up from the posterior longitudinal ligament. (Last's p. 557)
The foramen transversarium of the axis is vertical
It is directed up and out, bending the vertebral artery laterally. (Last's p. 557)
The axis transverse process represents the posterior tubercle of a typical cervical vertebra
Scalenus medius, splenius cervicis and levator scapulae attach to it. (Last's p. 557)
The superior articular facets of the axis lie entirely on the body
Each extends back onto the pedicle and out onto the lateral mass, overhanging the foramen transversarium. (Last's p. 557)
The apical ligament is a remnant of the notochord
The alar ligaments attach to the sloping borders of the dens. (Last's p. 557)
Failure of one half of the double centrum centre causes spina bifida
It causes hemivertebra. (Last's p. 557)
The spinal cord is narrower than the dura, and the dura narrower than the canal
So each adapts to movement without strain. (Last's p. 574)
Epidural fat extends into the intervertebral foramina around the root sleeves
(Last's p. 574)
The filum terminale pierces the theca at S2 and blends with periosteum on the back of the coccyx
(Last's p. 575)
The internal vertebral plexus is like a ladder whose rungs are the basivertebral veins
(Last's p. 574)
The centre for the anterior arch of the atlas appears at about 1 year
It fuses at 7. (Last's p. 558)
The lower articular facets of the atlas are deeply concave
They are circular and flat or very gently concave. (Last's p. 556)
The atlas transverse process usually shows distinct anterior and posterior tubercles
Usually there are none. (Last's p. 556)
The inferior articular facet of the axis faces upwards and backwards
It faces downwards and forwards. (Last's p. 557)
The spinous process of a typical cervical vertebra is single and rounded
It is usually bifid. (Last's p. 556)
The anterior longitudinal ligament is firmly attached to the front of the cervical bodies
Longus colli overlies it. (Last's p. 555)
The anterior longitudinal ligament spans the cervical basivertebral foramina
The posterior longitudinal ligament spans them. (Last's p. 555)
The bifid spine is excavated inferiorly by a pair of concavities for semispinalis
(Last's p. 556)
The sacral canal is triangular in cross-section
(Last's p. 554)
The meninges extend down to S2 within the sacral canal
(Last's p. 554)
The anterior surface of the male sacrum is gently and uniformly concave
The female is flat above and turns forward below. (Last's p. 554)
The fifth sacral foramen is bounded behind by the lateral sacral crest
It is formed behind by the cornua of sacrum and coccyx. (Last's p. 554)
